label: The Blood Gas and What Each Value Measures (Lecture 19)
rows: The arterial blood gas assesses OXYGENATION (oxygen), VENTILATION (carbon dioxide) and ACID-BASE status (pH, bicarbonate, carbon dioxide). Used with vital signs, the exam, a complete blood count and metabolic panel, intake and urine output.
Dissolved carbon dioxide: alveolar gas exchange, the rate and depth of breathing, alveolar ventilation. The major chemical driver of ventilation: as it rises, ventilation increases.
Oxygen DISSOLVED in plasma (less than 2%); 98% rides on hemoglobin. Directly affected by the fraction of inspired oxygen ("remember this"). Used to judge oxygenation and oxygen therapy.
A RATIO: hemoglobin's actual oxygen over its maximum capacity. The oxygen-hemoglobin relationship, not the content. Also measured by pulse oximetry.
The actual amount of oxygen in the blood (bound + dissolved).
Hemoglobin exposed to carbon monoxide (affinity 240 times oxygen's); indicates the amount of carbon monoxide poisoning. Normal under 2%.

Whole blood buffer base: bicarbonate is half, plasma proteins and phosphates the other half. Separates respiratory from nonrespiratory change. Positive = base excess; negative = base deficit (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis).
Volatile: carbonic acid. Nonvolatile: dietary, lactic, ketoacids (★ the classic ones).

label: The Oxygen-Hemoglobin Curve
rows: LEFT shift: hemoglobin holds on; oxygen bonds more tightly.
RIGHT shift: hemoglobin lets go; oxygen released more easily.
More hydrogen ions, more carbon dioxide, higher temperature, more BPG (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate).

label: Arterial Against Venous, and the Sample
rows: A better mixture of blood. Venous blood reflects its phlebotomy site (temperature, perfusion, movement, local infection).
What it shows, what it cannot
How well the lungs oxygenate and whether the heart and circulation are failing; NOT the degree of any abnormality: examine the patient.
Carbon dioxide higher (41 to 57), oxygen far lower (30 to 40), pH lower (7.31 to 7.41), content lower. Read each value against its own sample's range.
Radial artery usually; check collateral supply (ulnar and radial: the Allen test). No collateral = choose another site (femoral, brachial).
Collateral flow, superficial and accessible, non-sensitive surrounding tissue. Arterial line or direct stick.
Pre-heparinized syringe, air bubbles out, on ice; ★ note room air or supplemental oxygen; usable only under 3 hours; pressure at least 2 minutes.

label: When to Order an Arterial Blood Gas
rows: Oxygenation, ventilation, acid-base status; monitor response to therapy; monitor the critically ill; baseline before and after surgery.
The gas does not show severity. Do the labs fit the clinical presentation?

label: Reading the Gas, and Compensation
rows: 1 the pH (low acidosis, high alkalosis); 2 which values are out of range (the carbon dioxide next); 3 do the labs fit the patient?
Acidosis pH below 7.35; alkalosis above 7.45. Buffers: mainly lungs and kidneys (bones and blood less).
Retention from hypoventilation: obstructive lung disease; impaired respiratory center (anesthesia, narcotics, barbiturates, head trauma).
Hyperventilation: hypoxia, pulmonary emboli, ★ anxiety (the classic), pain, pregnancy.
Low atmospheric oxygen, cardiac dysfunction, shunts, obstructive or restrictive lung disease, edema, embolism, neuromuscular hypoventilation, too little inspired oxygen.
Kidney bicarbonate, over DAYS: acidosis bicarbonate up; alkalosis bicarbonate down.
Breathing and carbon dioxide, over MINUTES TO HOURS: acidosis carbon dioxide down; alkalosis carbon dioxide up.
Metabolic: pH, bicarbonate and carbon dioxide all move the same way. Respiratory: pH and carbon dioxide move opposite.

label: The Four Disorders
rows: pH low, carbon dioxide HIGH, bicarbonate normal: respiratory depression (opioids, barbiturates, anesthetics).
Carbon dioxide high, bicarbonate RISES, pH tries to normalize: long-standing lung or chest wall disease.
Chest wall (kyphoscoliosis), airway obstruction (extrathoracic tumor, asthma, bronchitis, emphysema), circulatory (heart failure, shock).
pH high, carbon dioxide LOW, bicarbonate normal: hyperventilation; brainstem stimulation (anxiety, fever, pregnancy); mild heart failure; mechanical over-ventilation.
Salicylates and sepsis: respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis. Severe heart failure: hypoperfusion, lactic acidosis.
pH low, carbon dioxide normal, bicarbonate LOW. Acid gain (renal failure, ★ ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, anaerobic metabolism) or base loss (diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis).
pH high, carbon dioxide normal, bicarbonate HIGH. Base gain (bicarbonate given), acid loss (vomiting, nasogastric suction), potassium or chloride depletion.
"Put a star on this slide": acidosis shifts potassium OUT of cells (hyperkalemia); alkalosis shifts it IN (hypokalemia).

label: The Anion Gap
rows: Anions other than chloride and bicarbonate; albumin is most of the normal gap.
Sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate). No potassium. Normal 9 to 15 (varies by source).
Usually MORE unmeasured anions (ketoacids, lactate, phosphate, albumin); less often FEWER unmeasured cations (calcium, magnesium, potassium, gamma-globulins).
More unmeasured cations (lithium); low albumin; severe hyperlipidemia (skews sodium and chloride).
Correct the gap if albumin is abnormal: ADD 2.5 for each 1 g/dL below 4.5.
